paragraphs: After hearing the order his father shouted from the carriage, Alyosha stood undecided for a while. But for all his uneasiness, he did not stay standing there. That was not his way. He went straight to the kitchen to find out what his father had been up to upstairs. Then he set off, trusting that somewhere on the road he would find an answer to the doubt that troubled him. I should add right away that his father’s shouts, telling him to come home “with his mattress and pillow,” did not frighten him in the least. He understood perfectly well that those domineering shouts were only “a flourish,” put on for effect. There was a tradesman in our town who did much the same thing. He was celebrating his name-day with a party of friends, and when they refused him more vodka, he got angry. He smashed his own crockery and furniture, tore his own clothes and his wife’s, and finally broke his own windows, all for effect. Next day, of course, once he was sober, he was sorry about the broken cups and saucers. Alyosha knew that his father would let him go back to the monastery the next day, maybe even that evening. Besides, he was completely sure that his father might hurt anyone else, but would never hurt him. Alyosha was certain that nobody in the whole world would ever want to hurt him. More than that, he knew that nobody could. For him this was an axiom, taken for granted once and for all, and he went on his way without hesitation, relying on it.

But now a different kind of anxiety was bothering him, and it worried him all the more because he could not put it into words. He was afraid of a woman, Katerina Ivanovna. In the note that Madame Hohlakov had handed him, she had urgently begged him to come and see her about something. The request, and the need to go, had stirred an uneasy feeling in his heart straight away. All morning that feeling had been growing more painful, in spite of the scenes at the hermitage and at the Father Superior’s. It was not that he was uneasy about what she would talk of, or what he ought to answer. Nor was he afraid of her simply because she was a woman. He knew little of women, but he had lived among women all his life, from early childhood until he entered the monastery. No, he was afraid of that particular woman, Katerina Ivanovna. He had been afraid of her since the first time he saw her. He had seen her only two or three times, and had happened to say only a few words to her. To him she was a beautiful, proud, commanding girl. It was not her beauty that troubled him, but something else. And because his dread was so vague, it only grew worse. He knew her aims were of the noblest. She was trying to save his brother Dmitri, out of pure generosity, even though Dmitri had already treated her badly. Alyosha saw all these fine and generous feelings, and gave them full credit. Still, a shiver began running down his back as soon as he got near her house.

He thought that he would not find Ivan there with her, though Ivan was such a close friend of hers, because Ivan was surely with their father by now. He was even more certain that Dmitri would not be there, and he had a foreboding of why. So he would be talking to her alone. He badly wanted to run and see his brother Dmitri before that fateful meeting. He could talk to Dmitri about it without showing him the letter. But Dmitri lived a long way off, and was bound to be out as well. Alyosha stood still for a minute and made his final decision. He crossed himself with a quick, habitual gesture, smiled at once, and turned resolutely toward his terrible lady.

He knew her house. Going by the High Street and then across the market-place was a long way round. Our town is small, but it is spread out, and the houses are far apart. Meanwhile his father was waiting for him, and might not yet have forgotten his order. He could be unreasonable, so Alyosha needed to hurry to get there and back. He decided, therefore, on a short cut through the back ways, since he knew every inch of the ground. That meant skirting fences, climbing over hurdles, and crossing other people’s back-yards, where everyone he met knew him and greeted him. By this route he could reach the High Street in half the time.

On the way he had to pass the garden next to his father’s. It belonged to a little tumbledown house with four windows. As Alyosha knew, the house belonged to a bedridden old woman who lived with her daughter. The daughter had been a genteel maid-servant in generals’ households in Petersburg, and had now been home for a year, nursing her sick mother. She always dressed up in fine clothes, although she and her old mother had fallen into such poverty that they went to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s kitchen every day for soup and bread, which Marfa gave them readily. And yet, for all that she came up for soup, the young woman had never sold any of her dresses. One of them even had a long train. Alyosha had learned this from Rakitin, who always knew everything that went on in town. He had forgotten it the moment he heard it. But now, as he reached the garden, he remembered the dress with the train. He lifted his head, which had been bowed in thought, and met with something quite unexpected.

Dmitri was standing on something behind the hurdle in the garden, leaning forward, waving his arms wildly and beckoning to him. He was clearly afraid to say a word in case he was overheard. Alyosha ran up to the hurdle.
“Good thing you looked up! I was almost shouting to you,” Mitya said in a happy, hurried whisper. “Climb in here, quick! How wonderful that you’ve come! I was just thinking of you!”

Alyosha was delighted too, but he did not know how to get over the hurdle. Mitya put his powerful hand under his elbow to help him jump. Alyosha tucked up his cassock and vaulted the hurdle as nimbly as a barefoot street boy.
“Well done! Now come along,” said Mitya in an excited whisper.
“Where to?” whispered Alyosha, looking around him. He was in a deserted garden with nobody near but the two of them. The garden was small, but the house was at least fifty paces away.
“There’s no one here. Why are you whispering?” asked Alyosha.

“Why am I whispering? Deuce take it!” cried Dmitri at the top of his voice. “You see what silly tricks nature plays on a man. I’m here in secret, on the watch. I’ll explain later. But since I know it’s a secret, I started whispering like a fool, when there’s no need. Let’s go. Over there. Till then, not a word. I want to kiss you.
Glory to God in the world, Glory to God in me ...
I was just saying that over, sitting here, before you came.”

The garden was about three acres, with trees planted only along the fence on all four sides: apple-trees, maples, limes and birches. The middle was an empty stretch of grass, which gave several hundredweight of hay in the summer. The owners rented the garden out for a few roubles for the summer. There were also patches of raspberries, currants and gooseberries along the sides, and a kitchen garden had recently been planted near the house.

Dmitri led his brother to the most secluded corner of the garden. In a thicket of lime-trees and old bushes of black currant, elder, snowball-tree and lilac stood a tumble-down green summer-house, blackened with age. Its walls were lattice-work, but it still had a roof that kept off the rain. God knows when it was built. The story was that a retired colonel named von Schmidt, who owned the house back then, had put it up some fifty years before. It was all falling to pieces. The floor was rotting, the planks were loose, and the woodwork smelled musty. Inside stood a green wooden table fixed in the ground, with green benches around it that were still safe to sit on. Alyosha had noticed his brother’s exhilarated state right away, and when he entered the arbor he saw half a bottle of brandy and a wineglass on the table.
“That’s brandy,” Mitya laughed. “I can see what you’re thinking: ‘He’s drinking again!’ Don’t trust appearances.
Don’t trust the worthless, lying crowd, And put your doubts aside.

I’m not drinking, I’m just ‘indulging,’ as that pig Rakitin of yours says. He’ll be a civil councilor one day, but he’ll still be talking about ‘indulging.’ Sit down. Alyosha, I could take you in my arms and press you to my chest until I crush you, because in the whole world—in reality—in re-al-i-ty—(can you take that in?) I love no one but you!”
He said the last words in a kind of exaltation.

“No one but you, and one ‘jade’ I’ve fallen in love with, to my ruin. But being in love isn’t the same as loving. You can be in love with a woman and hate her all the same. Remember that! I can still talk about it cheerfully. Sit down here at the table. I’ll sit beside you and look at you, and keep on talking. You keep quiet and I’ll talk, because the time has come. But on second thought, you know, I’d better keep my voice down, because here—here—you can never tell who’s listening. I’ll explain everything; as they say, ‘to be continued.’ Why have I been longing for you? Why have I been thirsting for you all these days, and just now? (It’s five days since I dropped anchor here.) Because you’re the only one I can tell everything to. Because I must, because I need you, because tomorrow I’ll tumble down from the clouds, because tomorrow life ends and begins. Have you ever felt, have you ever dreamed, that you were falling down a precipice into a pit? That’s exactly how I’m falling, only it isn’t a dream. And I’m not afraid, and you shouldn’t be afraid either. Well, I am afraid, but I enjoy it. Not enjoyment, though, but ecstasy. Damn it all, whatever it is! A strong spirit, a weak spirit, a womanish spirit—whatever it is! Let’s praise nature. Look at the sunshine, how clear the sky is, the leaves all green, still summer. Four o’clock in the afternoon, and such stillness! Where were you going?”
